articles.title: Comércio no Vale do Paraíba: queda nas vendas e esperança no Natal | G1
articles.standfirst: Setor fechou 1.590 postos de trabalho no primeiro semestre e registrou queda de 1,1% nas vendas; especialista explica cenário e perspectivas para os próximos meses.
articles.summary: O comércio no Vale do Paraíba fechou 1.590 postos de trabalho no primeiro semestre, mas setor projeta recuperação com as vendas de Black Friday e Natal.
articles.body:
O comércio do Vale do Paraíba desacelerou no primeiro semestre de 2026, mas o segundo período do ano pode trazer uma reação para o setor, principalmente com a chegada de datas como Dia das Crianças, Black Friday e Natal.

Entre janeiro e junho, o comércio da região fechou 1.590 postos de trabalho, segundo levantamento do Sindicato do Comércio Varejista de Taubaté e Região (Sincovat), com base nos dados do Cadastro Geral de Empregados e Desempregados (Caged).

Em São José dos Campos , foram 265 vagas a menos no comércio entre janeiro e julho. Apesar disso, a cidade teve saldo geral positivo de 2.712 empregos formais no período.

A redução no número de vagas acompanha uma queda nas vendas. O comércio movimentou R$ 38,8 bilhões no Vale no primeiro semestre, 1,1% menos do que no mesmo período de 2025.

Segundo o presidente do Sincovat, Dan Guinsburg, o cenário representa uma acomodação da economia. Mesmo com a queda, o faturamento registrado no primeiro semestre de 2026 foi o segundo maior da série histórica.

Comércio espera aumento nas vendas no segundo semestre, impulsionado por datas como Black Friday e Natal. — Foto: Reprodução/TV Vanguarda

Um dos setores mais afetados foi o de eletroeletrônicos, que depende mais do crédito para as compras.

Para Guinsburg, o endividamento e a inadimplência das famílias têm pesado sobre o consumo. Ele também chama atenção para o uso excessivo do cartão de crédito.

“Quem cai no rotativo do cartão de crédito fica numa situação muito complicada.”

Com menos espaço no orçamento, o consumidor tende a adiar compras de maior valor ou buscar alternativas mais baratas.

Outro fator é a mudança no comportamento de compra. As vendas pela internet ganharam força, principalmente em segmentos como roupas e eletroeletrônicos.

Para o presidente do Sincovat, os comerciantes precisam se adaptar a esse novo cenário e combinar a presença física com a digital.

“Não dá mais para ter só uma loja física, ela tem que estar tanto na internet como na física, se ela quiser sobreviver.”

Apesar do cenário de cautela, o comércio costuma ter um desempenho melhor no segundo semestre. Isso acontece principalmente por causa do calendário de vendas, que inclui Dia das Crianças, Black Friday e Natal.

“Segundo semestre sempre é melhor”, avalia Guinsburg, que afirma estar otimista com as vendas de fim de ano.

Para quem trabalha no comércio ou busca uma oportunidade no setor, o aumento do movimento nos próximos meses pode representar também uma possibilidade de novas contratações.

O desempenho, no entanto, dependerá do comportamento do consumidor e das condições de crédito nos próximos meses.

articles.title: Willington man guilty of killing his dad in pub garden
articles.summary: Martin Greensmith had only learnt Steven Shevels was his dad shortly before the fatal encounter.
articles.body:
A man who pushed over and killed his newly-discovered father in a pub garden on Christmas Eve has been found guilty of manslaughter.

Martin Greensmith, 37, only learnt Steven Shevels, 61, was his biological father shortly before their encounter behind The Queen's Head in Willington, County Durham, on 24 December, Teesside Crown Court heard.

Greensmith said he only "gently" pushed Shevels after the victim "intimidated" him , but prosecutors maintained he had caused his death during a fit of anger.

The defendant, who told jurors he was "very remorseful" and wanted to apologise to the victim's family, will be sentenced on 21 October.

Judge Jonathan Carroll remanded Greensmith into custody on the grounds of the "likely sentence" that would be imposed.

Jurors reached their verdict after almost six hours of deliberation, with 10 of the cohort of 12 finding him guilty.

Speaking after the verdict, Shevels' sister, Angela, said her brother was "the victim of an unprovoked act of violence that took his life far too soon".

His death had "left a hole in all our hearts" and a "future forever changed for all of his family, friends, and everyone who knew him", she added.

Jurors had heard how the Greensmith family had gone to The Queen's Head on the afternoon of 24 December, where Shevels was also drinking.

Greensmith told the court, although he knew his father was a man called Steven Shevels, it was not until his family were in the pub on Christmas Eve that his mother identified him.

Shevels, who the court heard was known in the town of Crook to be a nuisance when drunk, annoyed the Greensmith family by sitting nearby and trying to talk to them.

Greensmith said he went outside to get away from Shevels, but a few minutes later the victim also went out into the beer garden, having been asked to leave the pub, the jury heard.

The defendant told jurors he went to walk past Shevels, but the victim put his arm out to block him, and the pair exchanged a few short sentences, culminating with Greensmith telling the other man "something along the lines of 'you're my dad, I don't want to know you'".

He said Shevels moved closer to him, causing the accused to "gently" push the victim back to create space between them.

Greensmith said he was stunned to see Shevels fall over and was one of a number of people who tried to help up the stricken victim as he lay unconscious on the ground.

Despite the best efforts of those in the pub, including Greensmith's mother and paramedics, Shevels was pronounced dead at the scene about an hour later.

A pathologist told jurors he was killed by a blunt force trauma to the head, with a concussion causing him to lose consciousness and his alcohol consumption limiting his ability to keep breathing.

Greensmith left the pub before the emergency services attended, but handed himself into police at the home he shared with his mother at lunchtime on Christmas Day.

Before being arrested, Greensmith had made online searches for a lawyer and looked at a page with information on "involuntary manslaughter", the court heard.

Det Ch Insp Alfie Keane, of Durham Police, said it was a "truly devastating case".

"It shows how split-second decisions can have life-long consequences and an unimaginable impact on everyone around them," he said.

articles.title: VinFast pauses three India EV models over cost concerns – report
articles.summary: VinFast had asked suppliers to “hold all activities” on three programmes: the VF 3, a two-door SUV regarded as its most affordably priced offering for the In...
articles.body:
VinFast has reportedly suspended local manufacturing plans for three electric vehicle models in India, instructing suppliers to halt related work while the company reassesses costs.

Citing unnamed sources and an internal memo, Reuters reported that VinFast had asked suppliers to "hold all activities" on three programmes: the VF 3, a two-door SUV regarded as its most affordably priced offering for the Indian market, alongside the VF 6 and VF 7 SUVs.

The latter two are presently imported as kits from Vietnam for assembly within the country.

The development represents a setback roughly a year after VinFast, backed by Vietnamese conglomerate Vingroup, entered the Indian market in September 2025 with the launch of its VF 6 and VF 7 electric SUVs.

The company established its first factory outside Vietnam in southern India last year and committed to a $2bn investment as part of efforts to build a regional manufacturing hub serving South Asia, the Middle East and Africa.

According to a memo circulated to suppliers in July, VinFast had "temporarily" halted all development work linked to the VF 3, VF 6 and VF 7.

Suppliers were also asked to submit a detailed breakdown of the "total amount invested to date" across the three projects, encompassing tooling, engineering and material costs requiring payment or reimbursement, together with "supporting documentation where available".

One source indicated that VinFast had been unable to meet its intended cost targets for developing components locally, a shortfall that prompted the pause.

Sourcing components domestically had been intended to reduce reliance on costly imports and enable more competitive pricing within India.

Following the initial report, VinFast stated that the shift in production approach concerns future models, confirming it would continue importing and assembling the VF 6 and VF 7 currently available for sale in India.

The company added that it intends to develop models designed specifically for the Indian market rather than relying solely on existing global models, which it said would facilitate quicker local sourcing.

"India is an important market in VinFast's long-term business and manufacturing strategy," a company representative said, adding that it is making "appropriate adjustments" to its products, based on market research and customer feedback, to "better meet the needs of Indian customers".

VinFast has sold around 10,000 cars in India to date, including sales to its affiliate ride-hailing company Green SM.

"VinFast pauses three India EV models over cost concerns – report" was originally created and published by Just Auto , a GlobalData owned brand.

articles.title: 'Below the dignity of the office': Canadian officials condemn Pete Hegseth cadet post
articles.summary: The US Defence Secretary is facing criticism for his apparent online mocking of members of Canada's cadet programme.
articles.body:
US Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth is under fire in Canada for a social media post that appears to mock members of the country's cadet youth programme.

Hegseth posted the image, taken from the social media account for a local training branch, showing a young cadet receiving an award from her instructor.

He added a Canadian flag emoji and the caption "this is real" - an apparent attempt at disparaging Canada's military by making fun of the pair's appearance.

Canadian Defence Minister David McGuinty said on Tuesday that Hegseth's post was "below the dignity of the office".

The US and Canada are in the middle of a trade dispute that has often descended into a war of words, and the Trump administration has long accused their northern neighbour of relying on American military might for its defence.

Asked about the post and other recent jibes from Trump administration officials, Prime Minister Mark Carney said on Tuesday that any trade discussions would only begin again "when the Americans stop doing memes, stop throwing shade, stop trying to be tough and start being serious about having those discussions".

The Pentagon has said the post by Hegseth "speaks for itself".

The national cadet programme is overseen by the military and offers leadership and skills training to youth aged 12 to 18.

In a statement, the Army Cadet League of Canada, a civilian organisation that supports the programme, said it strongly condemns "any online harassment, or mockery of cadets' achievements".

"Directing derogatory commentary toward youth who are actively working to better themselves and serve their communities is unacceptable," the organisation said.

Speaking to broadcaster CBC, Canada's top military commander, General Jennie Carignan, said they are in contact with the cadets involved and any response they may have.

"We are consulting with them on how they want to go about doing this," she said.

Other officials weighed in, including Scott Anderson, a Conservative member of parliament for the Canadian city of Vernon and a former military reservist, who in a post directed at Hegseth accused him not living up to the "responsibility and decorum" that comes with his title.

"You have chosen to set both aside and insult two female Canadian non-combatants, and to intentionally shame them before millions. You should be ashamed," he said.

"Our economies, our continental defence and our cultures are irretrievably intertwined and yet we are two distinct nations. Canadians and Americans should have no problem with each other, but I have a problem with you," Anderson added.

A number of pundits and some Canadians accused the defence secretary of "body-shaming" with his post.

Trade talks broke down between Canada and the US last month, with both sides accusing the other of last-minute demands that torpedoed a tentative agreement.

The US immediately imposed 50% tariffs on some $20bn (C$28bn) of Canadian imports, and Canada plans to bring in matching countermeasures next week.

Both sides have traded insults, including Ontario Premier Doug Ford calling Trump a "loser", the US president seeking to change the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America , and transportation secretary Sean Duffy accusing Canada of being a country that "doesn't have a military".

Still, the two counties have long been defence partners and allies, including when Canada backed the US in the war in Afghanistan.

Canada has also significantly ramped up defence spending in recent months after years of lagging behind Nato targets.

Hegseth, a veteran, is himself under pressure at home following a string of recent high-profile military leaders leaving the Pentagon and questions about the US handling of the Iran war.

He has also long focused on the appearance and physical fitness of US troops and on what he calls the "warrior ethos".

articles.title: Israel kills or injures 7 children a day in Lebanon invasion, report says
articles.summary: Save the Children data shows toll on children in Lebanon, despite government agreement with Israel to halt fighting.
articles.body:
Israel has killed an average of seven children each day in Lebanon since March, according to the Save the Children relief organisation.

In a release on Wednesday, the group said that despite agreements between Lebanon’s government and Israel aimed at ending the fighting, children remain at risk due to Israel’s ongoing aggression towards civilian infrastructure.

Over the last six months, Israel has killed at least 4,300 people, wounded over 12,000 and destroyed between 60 and 70 villages, according to Save the Children. The toll includes at least 257 children killed and 1,039 injured.

Nora Ingdal, group’s Lebanon country director, said “The international community must not allow continued attacks, displacement, restrictions on return and the destruction of civilian infrastructure to become the new normal for children in Lebanon.”

At the peak of the fighting, more than a million people were displaced in southern Lebanon. Over 348,800 people remain unable to return home despite the ceasefire signed in June, according to the United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs.

Hezbollah and Israel began launching cross-border strikes following the Hamas-led attacks on southern Israel on October 7, 2023.

The two sides reached a tentative ceasefire agreement in November 2024 after Israel seized swathes of territory in southern Lebanon. Israeli forces have continued to occupy many areas in southern Lebanon and have repeatedly violated the ceasefire.

The deal largely collapsed after the Lebanon-based armed group Hezbollah launched a rocket and drone attack against a military base in northern Israel on March 2, in retaliation for the killing of Iranian Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei .

The Lebanese government and Israel reached a framework agreement to end the fighting in June, which Hezbollah has rejected unless Israel fully withdraws from Lebanese territory.

The two sides reached an earlier agreement aimed at ending the fighting in April.

Save the Children said that even for children who have been able to return to their homes in recent months, barriers to all forms of essential services, including schools and hospitals, persist.

A nationwide assessment conducted by Lebanon’s Ministry of Education and Higher Education has found that 340 schools have been damaged or destroyed in the past six months.

At least 100,000 children are at risk of missing the next school year without urgent action to restore Lebanon’s schools, according to Save the Children.

articles.title: US ambassador urges NATO vigilance: ‘You can’t predict what Vladimir Putin’s going to do’
articles.summary: Matthew Whitaker, the U.S. ambassador to NATO, is urging the military alliance’s members to boost defense spending and weapons production to prepare for emerging Russian threats. “You can’t predict what Vladimir Putin’s going to do or any adversary,” he told USA Today during an interview at NATO’s headquarters in Brussels, referring to the Russian president.…
articles.body:
Matthew Whitaker, the U.S. ambassador to NATO, is urging the military alliance’s members to boost defense spending and weapons production to prepare for emerging Russian threats.

“You can’t predict what Vladimir Putin’s going to do or any adversary,” he told USA Today during an interview at NATO’s headquarters in Brussels, referring to the Russian president.

“All you can do is be prepared for it and deter and make it not worth their time to make that move,” the ambassador continued. “And I think we are preparing every single day to prevent that from happening, and if it does happen, to be ready for it. We should know that our adversary invaded Ukraine, and so we should all be pretty clear-eyed.”

Whitaker’s call follows reporting from The Wall Street Journal last month on a leaked U.S. intelligence assessment that reportedly found Russia could attempt to launch a limited assault on a NATO country in the next few years.

A previous U.S. assessment predicted Putin would hold off an assault on a NATO-allied country while he was still engaged in a war against Ukraine. U.S. officials told the Journal the assessment shifted earlier this year amid increasing pressure in Russia to end the years-long conflict.

Whitaker declined to comment on this leaked report to USA Today, according to the outlet, instead focusing on calling on NATO nations to up defense spending.

“We need to exercise like it matters,” he told the publication. “We need to prepare, we need to invest in capabilities.”

NATO countries agreed last year to invest five percent of their annual gross domestic product in defense spending by 2035, including 3.5 percent for military spending.

Last week, CIA Director John Ratcliffe made a surprise visit to Moscow to warn Russia against launching an attack against NATO countries, the Journal first reported .

President Trump described the trip as “semi-routine” in an interview with conservative talk show host Glenn Beck, who pressed the president about whether Putin would “test NATO resolve.”

“John Ratcliffe is a fantastic guy,” Trump said. “He’s the head of the CIA, and he is not in there for any of the things you said.”

articles.title: Southwest Airlines is rolling out its first airport lounges

articles.body: For the first time in Southwest Airlines’ history, the air carrier will have its own lounges for passengers. Expected to open in late 2027, the first four new lounges will be located in Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, Baltimore/Washington International Thurgood Marshall Airport, Daniel K. Inouye (Honolulu) International Airport and Nashville International Airport, Southwest Airlines said in a release on Wednesday. The airline will partner with the banking brand Chase to “create a premium and welcoming airport experience.” “Our lounges will be a natural extension of that experience, offering customers a place to relax and experience the Southwest brand in a new way,” said Tony Roach, executive vice president, chief customer & brand officer at Southwest Airlines, in the release. At least seven more lounges are planned to open in the next several years, the airline said. Travelers can gain access to the lounges by obtaining a new, premium Southwest Rapid Rewards Credit Card issued by Chase, launching next year. Passengers can expect the sort of design, dining, travel benefits and amenities that are currently offered in the Chase Sapphire Reserve Lounge Network, the airline said. The announcement comes as Southwest Airlines has had a tumultuous few years of change following an activist investor campaign to create profitability. Recent changes have included ending both open-seat boarding and the airline’s “bags fly free” policy, practices that distinguished Southwest from other airlines.

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln reaches Thailand after 9 months at sea
articles.summary: The port visit comes amid reports of severe emotional strain and poor conditions on board following nine months at sea.
articles.body:
United States Navy aircraft carrier USS Abraham Lincoln made port in eastern Thailand in the crew’s first port call after nine and a half months at sea, following a taxing deployment in the Middle East amid reports of supply issues, deteriorating mental health conditions and low morale on board.

Carrying a crew of 5,000, the nuclear-powered aircraft carrier was seen making its way into the Laem Chabang port in Chonburi province early on Wednesday, shortly after the destroyer USS Frank E Petersen Jr sailed past the area, accompanied by other US naval vessels.

By afternoon, busloads of plainclothes sailors and Marines arrived at a resort hotel in Pattaya, a coastal city 150 kilometres (93 miles) southeast of Bangkok. Thai officials have said the Lincoln’s stop would be for rest and recovery before returning to its US base.

The Lincoln had been anchoring the US naval blockade and combat operations during the US-Israeli war on Iran.

While crew members remained out of reach for comment, the ship’s weathered hull was noticeable, and the ship itself looked due for at least a new paint job, according to The Associated Press (AP) journalists who were present on-site. Large rust patches blemished the exterior, particularly along the waterline and the edge of the flight deck where fighters and helicopters sat parked.

When asked about the aircraft carrier’s lacklustre appearance, Captain Dan Keeler, the Lincoln’s commanding officer, replied that “it is normal for a long deployment” and declined to comment further.

US President Donald Trump rejected concerns raised by families of the Lincoln’s crew members over the aircraft carrier’s winding deployment for weeks. Standard naval deployments span six to nine months, extending only during periods of heightened conflict. Weeks ago at Joint Base Andrews, the home base for Air Force One, reporters had asked the president if the Lincoln had been at sea for too long. He responded , “No, not nearly long enough.”

Questioned about his thoughts regarding Trump’s earlier remarks, the commanding officer said: “So, the president speaks for himself.”

He told AP, “That is what I think about that.”

The sailors and Marines are expected to rest in Thailand for several days.

“Our arrival in Laem Chabang provides a well-deserved opportunity for our Sailors and Marines to rest and recharge,” the commander of Carrier Strike Group 3, Rear Admiral Robert E Loughran, said in a statement. “What this strike group has accomplished is truly historic. I could not be prouder of the exceptional professionalism and expertise demonstrated by every member of this team during our operations.”

During his second term, Trump pledged to steer clear of protracted, high-cost military conflicts. And after launching a joint war with Israel against Iran, the president and his advisers said the conflict would only last a matter of weeks. The war has now entered its seventh month.

articles.summary: A 21-foot steel beam from the South Tower of the World Trade Center heads to Fenway Park, D.C., and MetLife Stadium for the 9/11 anniversary.
articles.body: A 21-foot steel beam recovered from the South Tower of the World Trade Center will make its way up the East Coast this week as part of the Tunnel to Towers Foundation’s Steel Across America tour. The tour kicked off earlier this year as a way to mark the 25th anniversary of the 9/11 terrorist attacks and celebrate American service members and first responders. The steel will stop in Massachusetts, Washington, D.C., and New York City through Sept. 11. Wednesday night's stop will be at the Boston Red Sox vs. Seattle Mariners game at Fenway Park in Boston, before heading to the Massachusetts Fallen Heroes Memorial on Thursday. AMERICA’S HEARTLAND COMES FACE-TO-FACE WITH 9/11 HISTORY AS 25TH ANNIVERSARY NEARS The 16,900-pound beam will then head to the nation's capital, where it will be featured at a private event on Friday. It will then head to New York City for another private event in Brooklyn on Sept. 11, before a final appearance at the New York Giants vs. Dallas Cowboys game at MetLife Stadium on Sept. 13. The beam visited the U.S. Military Academy at West Point on Monday, where the superintendent, Lt. Gen. James B. Bartholomees III, said the piece of steel connects the courage shown by first responders on 9/11 with the Americans who answered the call to serve in the years that followed. The ceremony brought together cadets, faculty, staff and guests and opened with a color guard and pipe and drum procession by members of the NYPD, FDNY and Port Authority Police Department. articles.title: Daphne Caruana Galizia: Maltese tycoon acquitted of orchestrating journalist's murder
articles.summary: Daphne Caruana Galizia exposed corruption and money laundering schemes in Malta before she was killed by a car bomb in 2017.
articles.body:
A Maltese businessman on trial over the murder of investigative journalist Daphne Caruana Galizia has been acquitted.

Yorgen Fenech, 44, was accused of complicity in her murder and criminal association to commit murder. He denied all the charges.

In 2022, brothers George and Alfred Degiorgio were jailed for 40 years over the killing of Caruana Galizia, who was an outspoken critic of the government and had uncovered networks of corruption in Malta and abroad.

She was killed by a car bomb in October 2017, with speculation at the time that senior establishment figures may have been involved.

Fenech was cleared of both counts by an 8-1 margin after eight hours of deliberation by the jury, the Reuters news agency reported.

His family members screamed with delight in the packed courtroom in Valletta, while Caruana Galizia's family wept, the agency said.

"Nine years after Daphne's brutal assassination, the institutional failures that enabled her murder remain unaddressed and unreformed," her family said in a statement reported by local media.

"Lasting justice means no person should ever face the same risks again. Our country failed to protect Daphne's life. It owes it to her to prevent other lives being lost."

Daphne Caruana Galizia gained international prominence for her investigations into corruption, money laundering and organised crime, which she published on her blog Running Commentary.

She was deeply involved in the 2016 Panama Papers investigation - a cache of confidential documents leaked from a Panamanian law firm. The investigation exposed offshore structures and triggered corruption allegations directed at top government officials in Malta.

Her shocking assassination prompted widespread public outrage and protests on the streets of Malta at the time. She was 53 years old.

During the trial, the jury heard that Fenech had wanted the journalist killed because she was about to reveal information about him.

One of Malta's richest men, Fenech is a well-known figure and was the owner of a company Caruana Galizia had written about months before her death.

Fenech denied the accusations, and during the trial he deflected blame towards his one-time close friend Keith Schembri, former chief of staff of then-prime minister Joseph Muscat and a target of Caruana Galizia's stories.

Muscat, who was never linked to the murder, stepped down in January 2020 due to the political fallout from the assassination.

Police told the court that Schembri had never been a suspect, and he has denied any role in the murder.

In 2025, two men - Robert Agius and Jamie Vella - were jailed for life by a Maltese judge for having supplied the bomb.

articles.title: US says it will use regional body to isolate Nicaragua
articles.summary: Move comes after Nicaragua’s lawmakers change constitution to ban most political opposition.
articles.body:
The United States will use the Organization of American States (OAS) to isolate the Nicaraguan government over constitutional changes that have “gutted what was left” of democracy there.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio announced the move in a statement on Wednesday, saying Nicaraguan President Daniel Ortega and his wife and co-President Rosario Murillo were waging a “war on democracy” that “threatens our hemisphere’s stability and prosperity”.

The US would use an upcoming meeting of the OAS to urge countries in the hemisphere to stop doing “business as usual” with Nicaragua, he said.

Rubio’s comments come after Nicaraguan lawmakers on Tuesday passed a constitutional reform ‌package that largely ⁠bans opposition parties from participating in elections and extends the presidential term from six ⁠to seven years, an initiative that had previously drawn criticism ⁠from the US and other countries ⁠in the region.

Last month, the OAS decided to convene a meeting over the situation in Nicaragua, declaring that it was “a problem of an urgent nature and of common interest to the American States”.

Nicaragua said it had withdrawn from the regional body in 2022, after it repeatedly criticised the Ortega government’s human rights record. At the time, Nicaragua’s foreign minister lauded the withdrawal by saying the country was no longer part “of all the deceitful mechanisms of this monstrosity, the so-called Permanent Council, so-called commissions, so-called meetings, so-called Summit of the Americas”. The withdrawal fully went into effect in 2023.

The Washington-based OAS was founded with US backing in 1948 to promote international cooperation in the Western Hemisphere. Venezuela, under former President Nicolas Maduro, began the process of its withdrawal in 2017 after the body criticised his government’s handling of political unrest. Maduro’s foreign minister at the time, Delcy Rodriguez, called the OAS an “interventionist coalition” led by the US.

In July, Nicaragua’s Ortega government sent a draft constitutional reform package to lawmakers that it said would exclude “traitors” and “coup-plotting” opposition members from elections, and extend the presidential term from six to seven “renewable” years. It would also dissolve political parties that received funding from abroad.

“There won’t be ⁠⁠any more elections here for them to try to seize the government and seize power,” Ortega said after the changes were proposed, speaking during an event commemorating the 1979 Sandinista revolution that first brought him into power.

Ortega, a former Marxist rebel, helped overthrow the US-backed right-wing dictatorship of Anastasio Somoza. He led the post-revolutionary military government in Nicaragua until 1985, when he became president of the country, a role he held until 1990. In 2007, Ortega returned to power and is currently the longest-serving leader in the Western Hemisphere.

More than 300 people were killed in a crackdown after student-led protests against Ortega’s government in 2018. Ortega then jailed political opponents and journalists, eventually sending hundreds of them into exile and stripping them of their Nicaraguan citizenship. At least 200 of those sent into exile settled in the US.

articles.title: In 2005, Gateway co-founder Ted Waitt left the computer business and turned his fortune toward the oceans; his foundation has invested $70 million in marine conservation
articles.summary: US News: In 2005, Ted Waitt made a decisive shift away from the computer industry that had made him wealthy and towards a very different frontier of the world’.
articles.body: In 2005, Ted Waitt made a decisive shift away from the computer industry that had made him wealthy and towards a very different frontier of the world’s oceans. The co-founder of Gateway had spent years building one of America’s most recognisable personal computer companies, but after retiring from the business, he increasingly dedicated his time and resources to philanthropy and marine conservation. Since then, the Waitt Foundation has invested more than $70 million in ocean conservation initiatives, according to Waitt Institute. Through the Waitt Foundation, Waitt Institute and Blue Prosperity Coalition, his work has supported ocean research, marine protection and long-term planning with governments and local communities. The transformation represents a unique second act for a tech entrepreneur, one that moved from selling computers to tackling the growing challenge of protecting the planet’s increasingly pressured seas.Ted Waitt’s $70 million shift from computers to ocean conservationTed Waitt became wealthy through the rapid growth of Gateway, the computer company he helped build into a major name during the personal computer boom. According to EBSCO, Gateway began as the Texas Instruments Personal Computers Network in 1985 before becoming Gateway 2000 and later simply Gateway. The company grew quickly. EBSCO reports that Gateway reached $1 billion in sales in 1992 and was identified as the fastest-growing company in the United States. Waitt’s business success eventually made him one of the country’s most prominent technology entrepreneurs. However, his career at Gateway was not a straightforward climb. After stepping away from leadership, he returned to help the company through financial difficulties before retiring again in 2005, according to EBSCO. That departure marked a more permanent change in direction. The Waitt Institute says that since 2005, Waitt has dedicated much of his time and resources to the oceans through the Waitt Institute, Waitt Foundation and Blue Prosperity Coalition.Why did the oceans become Ted Waitt’s new focusThe Waitt Foundation describes the depletion of ocean resources as one of the biggest challenges facing the current generation. After leaving the computer business, Waitt turned his attention towards helping address that problem. According to the Waitt Foundation, the organisation has invested more than $70 million in ocean conservation projects, particularly those involving marine protected areas. It has also supported ocean research, policy and other efforts connected to the protection and management of marine resources. The scale of this commitment reflects a striking change from Waitt’s earlier career. His first fortune was built through personal computers. His later work has centred on the health and future of the oceans. The Waitt Foundation says Waitt has also sponsored dozens of marine science expeditions, with research taking place across all five oceans and all seven continents. These expeditions have formed part of his wider interest in understanding the marine environment.The conservation work combines science with practical planningWhile the Waitt Foundation provides funding, the Waitt Institute works directly with governments and communities. According to the Institute, it partners with committed governments and local communities to create sustainable ocean plans that can benefit people, economies and the environment. Its work includes support for policymaking, scientific assessments, technical expertise and planning tools. The Institute focuses on areas such as marine spatial planning, sustainable fisheries and the blue economy. This approach recognises that the ocean is not simply a wilderness separated from human life. Coastal waters support fishing, tourism and local livelihoods, meaning environmental decisions can have economic and social consequences as well. The Waitt Institute’s partnerships include the Azores, Bermuda, the Federated States of Micronesia, Fiji, Samoa, Tonga and Vanuatu.How does the Blue Prosperity Coalition support this workThe Waitt Institute says the Waitt Foundation funds both the Institute and the Blue Prosperity Coalition, which was launched in 2019. The Coalition brings together non-governmental organisations(NGOs), academic institutions, foundations and other partners. By combining expertise from different groups, it aims to support governments and communities in developing ways to manage ocean resources responsibly. The Waitt Foundation provides financial backing, the Waitt Institute works on partnerships and technical planning, while the Blue Prosperity Coalition brings additional organisations and expertise into the process. Rather than relying on a single method, the structure combines funding, science, planning and collaboration. This allows the work to address both the environmental pressures facing the oceans and the practical realities of communities that depend on them.From a technology fortune to a long-term ocean missionWaitt’s philanthropic interests began before his final departure from Gateway. EBSCO notes that he established the Waitt Foundation in 1993, initially supporting charitable activities in Sioux City and the surrounding region. Over time, the Foundation broadened its work, eventually placing a stronger emphasis on ocean conservation. Its activities have included support for marine protected areas, fisheries management and sustainability, according to the Foundation. However, the period after 2005 marked a major change in Waitt’s personal direction. The Waitt Institute says his commitment since then has included funding, scientific expeditions and partnerships aimed at improving how ocean resources are understood and managed.His journey from Gateway co-founder to ocean philanthropist shows how wealth created in one industry can be redirected towards an entirely different challenge. The personal computer business helped establish Waitt’s fortune and public profile, but the oceans became the defining focus of his later work. More than two decades after he left Gateway, the organisations founded and supported by Waitt continue to pursue long-term solutions for the seas. The Waitt Foundation’s investment demonstrates the scale of that commitment, turning one entrepreneur’s post-business career into an enduring effort focused on the future of the oceans.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: “People couldn’t make any money on YouTube”: Asmongold supports ad blockers despite calling them ‘stealing’
articles.summary: US Streamers News: Twitch and Kick streamer Zack “Asmongold” has shared an unusual view on ad blockers. The streamer said he believes blocking advertisements is “undenia.
articles.body: Twitch and Kick streamer Zack “Asmongold” has shared an unusual view on ad blockers. The streamer said he believes blocking advertisements is “undeniably an unethical behavior” because viewers are avoiding the form of compensation used to support online creators. However, Asmongold also admitted that he supports using ad blockers. During a recent Just Chatting stream, he explained why he sees the practice as technically unethical while still understanding why people choose to do it. He also discussed what could happen to online content if almost everyone blocked advertisements.Asmongold explains why he considers ad blocking unethicalA 1-minute-38-second clip from Asmongold’s recent stream surfaced on X on September 1, 2026. In the clip, a viewer asked whether he supported ad blockers or considered their use a form of “stealing.”Asmongold gave a direct answer.“I think I support ad blocking, and it is stealing. That's my opinion. I think ad blocking is undeniably an unethical behavior. There is no universe in which ad block is ethical.”He then explained that he does not believe people should pretend there is nothing wrong with avoiding advertisements while consuming free online content.“And I've always said, ‘If you're going to steal, steal. But steal with a smile and don't tell me you're Robin Hood.’”Asmongold’s main argument was based on what he described as a “social contract” between content creators and their audiences.He said:“Every single piece of media on the internet, you are entering into a social contract with the person who's providing that media, that you will provide them with some degree of collateral, or some degree of restitution, for consuming their labor or their input or whatever they're doing; their creation.”He argued that intentionally blocking advertisements removes part of that exchange.“Whenever you intentionally forego that, you know, basically that social contract that you have with that other person, you are making a world to where, if everybody did that, the content and the material that you are consuming could not exist.”For Asmongold, the issue is therefore less about one viewer blocking an advertisement and more about what could happen if the practice became universal.Asmongold says most YouTube creators could lose money if everyone used ad blockersAsmongold then applied the same argument to YouTube and other platforms that rely on advertising revenue.“Like, if everybody was using an ad block, most people couldn't make any money on YouTube, and the majority of videos on YouTube itself might just simply, you know, stop existing.”However, he acknowledged that the situation is not completely straightforward. He pointed to problematic advertisements as one reason viewers may choose to block ads.“Don't get me wrong here. Right? There are counterarguments to this, such as, ‘Well, what about scam ads? Do I have an obligation to show scam ads?’”He described the issue as a series of problems that have developed as internet advertising has changed.“And so, this is a Russian nesting doll of problems because we've had a lot of evolutions of it.”Despite those complications, Asmongold returned to his original position.“However, I think on a very baseline level, ad block is unethical, and I support using ad block.”His comments put him in an unusual position. He considers ad blocking morally wrong but still supports the choice to use it, particularly when users have concerns about the advertisements being shown to them.The discussion comes shortly after Asmongold made another widely discussed comment about fellow streamer Steven “Destiny” Bonnell II. Asmongold said that he, Felix “xQc” Lengyel and Hasan “HasanAbi” Piker might not have become the creators they are today without Destiny’s early influence on livestreaming. He specifically credited Destiny with helping establish non-gaming content on Twitch.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Judge sets $250,000 bail for accused Penn State cocaine trafficking ringleader
articles.summary: A judge set bail on Wednesday for the former Penn State fraternity brother at the center of an alleged cocaine trafficking ring.
articles.body: A judge set bail on Wednesday for the former Penn State fraternity brother at the center of an alleged cocaine trafficking ring. Centre County President Judge Jonathan Grine set bail at $250,000 for Agostino Abbatiello, according to online court records. As of Wednesday afternoon, Abbatiello has not posted bail, the records show. His attorney, Philip Masorti, did not immediately return a request for comment. Abbatiello, 24, appeared at a hearing at the Centre County Courthouse in Bellefonte, Pennsylvania, roughly 10 miles north of the university. He wore a red jumpsuit and was handcuffed and escorted into the courthouse by police officers. He was arrested last month and charged with felony corrupt organizations, conspiracy, and dealing in proceeds of unlawful activity. Prosecutors allege Abbatiello was the main supplier for the trafficking ring, selling other fraternity members cocaine in amounts ranging from small quantities to as much as a kilogram, according to court documents. Thirteen other people were arrested in connection with the case, including current and former students and the father of a former student. Several co-defendants — including Thomas Michael Robinson, Mohammed Huraibi and Lars Zeepvat — waived their preliminary hearings and instead testified against Abbatiello at his bail hearing, according to NBC affiliate WJAC-TV. A State College Police detective also testified, describing the alleged cocaine packaging operation involving the fraternities’ pledges, according to WJAC-TV. Unlike his co-defendants, Abbatiello was initially denied bail and has since been held at the Centre County Correctional Facility in Bellefonte. His attorney filed an emergency motion seeking bail, calling the denial “absurd” and disputing that Abbatiello posed a threat to the community. “After a two-year investigation, law enforcement never once asserted the Defendant used violence, threatened violence, or was ever seen with any weapon,” the motion states. In the same filing, Masorti also accused prosecutors of judge-shopping the case. The Pennsylvania Attorney General’s Office did not immediately return a request for comment. When they announced the charges last month, prosecutors described the alleged ring as a “coordinated and highly profitable” cocaine-trafficking operation. The investigation centers on two fraternities, Sigma Chi and Delta Upsilon. Abbatiello was a member of Sigma Chi, which Penn State says it has officially recognized for years. The fraternity has said it suspended its Penn State chapter following the arrests. Court documents accuse Abbatiello of enlisting fraternity brothers and pledges to package the drugs, according to an affidavit supporting the criminal complaint, and alleges he paid the men hundreds of dollars to act as couriers and replenish his supply. Abbatiello was born and raised in Nassau County, Long Island. Before Penn State, he attended Chaminade High School, a competitive all-boys Catholic school, where he played football for two years, according to court records. He graduated from Penn State in spring 2024 with a 3.3 GPA, according to court documents. At the time of his arrest, he was living in Boca Raton, Florida, and working as a financial advisor. He returned to State College and turned himself in to authorities on August 18, the records show. Court records indicate Abbatiello wants to live with his parents on Long Island while the case is pending.

articles.title: Airline involved in low stadium flyover turns over black box data as investigators probe if safety rules were violated
articles.summary: The airline behind a remarkably low planned flyover of a packed rugby stadium said Wednesday it will turn over data from the planes’ black boxes to show the maneuver was done in accordance with governmental rules.
articles.body: The airline behind a remarkably low planned flyover of a packed rugby stadium said Wednesday it will turn over data from the planes’ black boxes to show the maneuver was done in accordance with governmental rules. The two 98-seat Embraer-190 regional jets from South African airline Airlink buzzed Cape Town’s DHL stadium on Saturday just before the match between the country’s Springboks and New Zealand’s All Blacks teams. The planes’ lowest altitude was only about 46 feet above the roof of the stadium, according to the tracking website Flightradar 24. “The data recorded by both aircrafts’ digital flight data recorders (black boxes) indicate that the flights were performed within the (South African Civil Aviation Authority’s) approved and rehearsed safety altitude and speed limits for the fly-past,” Airlink said in a statement to CNN on Wednesday. The airline said authorities provided “guidance, approval and support to ensure a safe flyby,” and each of the planes were flown by three senior captains, including one who acted as a safety/technical officer. No passengers were onboard. The aviation authority is examining the flight data and requested additional information from Airlink, The Associated Press reported. “It is therefore critical that we interrogate this past weekend’s events… to determine if there were any safety concerns which warrant a review,” the agency said in a statement to the AP. Airlink staged a similar flyby over Johannesburg’s Ellis Park stadium one week earlier, using the same specially painted jets celebrating “rugby’s greatest rivalry.” The airline withdrew an application for a third flyover, citing bad weather, the AP reported. Many in South Africa, which the US has determined meets international standards for aviation oversight, have celebrated the flyover. “It’s a well known fact that we have the best pilots in the world, that was spectacular, next time I will ask the pilots to land on the field, prepare to be amazed further,” the South African Minister of Sport, Arts and Culture Gayton McKenzie joked online shortly after the flyover. “We are cooking something,” he posted Wednesday standing in front of another Airlink jet. Many aviation experts believe the flight was not worth the risk, with the extremely low altitude leaving no margin for error. “It was a very unsafe procedure and not necessary,” former NTSB chairman Pete Goelz told CNN. “A flyby at 1,000 ft is already impressive, and people enjoy it, and there’s no reason to lower it other than unnecessary risk taking.” United States rules say a plane must remain at least a thousand feet above congested areas, unless it has explicit permission from the Federal Aviation Administration. Low-flying airliners are, however, part of South African rugby history. In 1995, a South African Airways Boeing 747 famously flew over the Rugby World Cup final in Johannesburg. And in 2024, an Emirates A380 flew over the same stadium, though a few hundred feet higher. Saturday’s flyover in Cape Town punctuates a summer of aircraft flying stunningly close to the ground. In July, a pilot from the U.S. Navy’s Blue Angels flew low over the crowd during the Pensacola Beach air show, sending tents flying and military leaders scrambling to defend the maneuver. A month before, a Boeing 777 on a test flight passed as low as 25 feet over a runway at Horseshoe Bay, Texas, triggering a federal investigation.

articles.title: DOJ says states have to report undocumented immigrants to get federal funding
articles.summary: The Justice Department issued a new legal interpretation on Wednesday in an attempt to push every state in the country to report undocumented immigrants living in their communities and advance President Donald Trump’s mass deportation plan.
articles.body: The Justice Department issued a new legal interpretation on Wednesday in an attempt to push every state in the country to report undocumented immigrants living in their communities and advance President Donald Trump’s mass deportation plan. The department’s Office of Legal Counsel, which advises the Attorney General, said that when states accept federal funds to assist low-income families — through the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families and the Supplemental Security Income programs — they’re obligated to report anyone who’s not lawfully present in the U.S. to the Department of Homeland Security, according to its new legal opinion. The reporting requirement would extend to the entire state government, not just the agencies administering TANF and SSI benefits, according to the opinion. Every state in the country receives federal funding to provide financial assistance through both programs — which are among the nation’s largest safety net programs for low-income families, elderly residents and disabled people. The Office of Legal Counsel said it reinterpreted a Clinton-era opinion from 1998 that required only the specific state agencies tasked with overseeing TANF or SSI programs to share information federal immigration authorities. “States will not face retroactive penalties for past reliance on the 1998 interpretation,” the DOJ said in a news release Wednesday, but it expects states to abide by the new opinion in the future. It’s likely that certain states, especially those that are led by Democrats, will challenge the new legal interpretation in court. State attorneys general in several states have already pushed back on prior attempts from the Trump administration to force local agencies to share information regarding immigration status with the federal government alongside other immigration enforcement efforts.

articles.title: Uber shuts operations in Nigeria and Uganda with immediate effect
articles.summary: Nigeria - Africa's most populous country - is proving a tough market for ride-hailing services.
articles.body:
Uber has announced it is closing its operations in Nigeria - Africa's most populous country - and the East African nation of Uganda with immediate effect

The global ride-hailing giant said it had come to the "difficult decision" after a thorough review of its business. It began operating in Nigeria in 2014 and in Uganda two years later.

Uber taxi drivers in Nigeria have long complained that prices on the app are too low, given the rising cost of fuel, and that commission charges are too high. The company has also faced pressure from rival platforms.

The announcement came as Uber's chief executive, Dara Khosrowshahi, said the company was cutting its global workforce by 10%.

Uber to cut over 3,000 jobs in major global restructuring

Over the last year, Uber has also pulled out of Ivory Coast and Tanzania. The latest announcement means Egypt, Ghana, Kenya and South Africa are the only African countries in which the firm now operates.

"This decision is limited strictly to these two markets and does not impact our operations across the rest of the continent," Uber's statement to the BBC said.

"We remain committed to sub-Saharan Africa, where we continue to see strong growth and opportunity."

Over its 12 years operating in Nigeria, Uber had expanded its services. In the commercial hub of Lagos, it launched a boat service in 2019 in an effort to help commuters bypass the city's notorious congestion.

Lagos, one of Africa's largest and busiest cities, is infamous for its long traffic jams that cause gridlock and hamper business activity.

Other ride-hailing taxi apps have launched in the West African nation over the last decade, including international competitors such as Bolt and inDrive, as well as a number of local operators.

But the Nigerian market has become increasingly challenging for them all, with drivers staging protests and industrial action in recent years over rising operating costs, low fares and working conditions.

The removal of Nigeria's fuel subsidy after President Bola Tinubu's election in 2023 saw the cost of living rise. The subsidy had kept down the price of petroleum products low for decades.

This year, motorists have been hit again by the rise in petrol prices following the US's war with Iran.

Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper said Uber's departure would mean a major change for commuters in the capital, Kampala. But it said the void was likely to be filled by other taxi apps such as Faras, Bolt and SafeBoda.

Uber pledged to support employees and drivers affected by the decision and said its help centre would remain open for those in Nigeria and Uganda until 23 September to deal with outstanding issues.

articles.title: A Wisconsin farming family fought a 2016 tax change as nearly 2,000 floodplain acres became harder to farm; 10 years later, the land is being permanently protected
articles.summary: US News: For generations, the Hoesly family farmed rich bottomland along the Wisconsin and Kickapoo rivers in southwest Wisconsin, growing corn and soybeans on.
articles.body: For generations, the Hoesly family farmed rich bottomland along the Wisconsin and Kickapoo rivers in southwest Wisconsin, growing corn and soybeans on nearly 2,000 acres of floodplain. But as floods grew more frequent and severe, and a 2016 state tax change made it harder to claim agricultural exemptions on frequently inundated land, the family found themselves fighting to keep the farm viable. A decade later, instead of doubling down on drainage and levees, they have chosen a different path: working with conservation groups and the state to permanently protect the land as floodplain forest and wildlife habitat. As reported by The Daily Cardinal, the deal marks one of the largest private conservation agreements in recent Wisconsin history and a quiet admission that some land is better left to the river.A family tied to the floodplainThe Hoesly family’s roots in the region go back more than a century. Their ancestors homesteaded on the fertile river bottoms, drawn by the deep soils and reliable moisture that made the land ideal for row crops. Over time, the farm grew to include close to 2,000 acres spread across multiple parcels along the Wisconsin and Kickapoo rivers, near the town of Wauzeka.For decades, the family managed the land like many Midwestern farmers: clearing brush, maintaining drainage ditches, building up levees and planting corn and soybeans in the short windows between floods. When the rivers stayed in their banks, the bottomland produced bumper crops. When they didn’t, the family absorbed the losses and replanted.When floods became the normIn the 2000s and 2010s, the pattern began to shift. Heavy rain events grew more frequent, and the rivers rose higher and more often. Fields that once flooded every few years were underwater every other spring, sometimes multiple times in a single growing season. Crops drowned, equipment got stuck, and the cost of repairing levees and ditches climbed.The Hoeslys, like many farmers in the region, found themselves in a cycle of damage and repair that was increasingly hard to justify economically. Insurance payouts and federal disaster assistance helped, but they did not cover the full cost of lost yields, delayed planting and damaged infrastructure.The 2016 tax change that tipped the scalesIn 2016, Wisconsin adjusted how it applied agricultural property tax exemptions to floodplain land. Under the new rules, it became harder to classify frequently flooded acres as “agricultural” for tax purposes if they could not be reliably cropped year after year. For the Hoeslys, who already struggled with unpredictable harvests, the change meant higher property taxes on land that was increasingly unprofitable to farm, as per the report.The family pushed back, arguing that they were still actively managing the land for agriculture and that the tax shift punished farmers for climate-driven flooding they could not control. But the assessments stood, and the financial pressure mounted. By the early 2020s, the Hoeslys were facing a stark choice: invest even more in flood control infrastructure on land that might never be reliably dry, or reconsider the long-term future of the farm.A different vision for the bottomlandAs the family weighed their options, they began talking with conservation organisations, state agencies and neighbouring landowners about alternative uses for the floodplain. The conversations centred on a few key ideas: Much of the land had historically been floodplain forest and wetland before it was cleared for farming; restoring native vegetation could reduce flood risks downstream by allowing water to spread out and slow down; and protected floodplain habitat would benefit fish, waterfowl, deer and other wildlife, while also creating opportunities for hunting, fishing and recreation.For a farming family, this was a significant shift in mindset. But the Hoeslys began to see conservation not as a surrender, but as a way to honour the land’s natural character while securing its future.The conservation dealAfter several years of negotiations, the Hoesly family agreed to place nearly 2,000 acres of floodplain into permanent protection through a combination of conservation easements and land donations. Key partners in the deal include: The Wisconsin Department of Natural Resources (DNR), which will manage much of the land as part of the state’s natural areas and wildlife management system; nonprofit conservation groups, such as the Wisconsin Land and Water Conservation Trust and local land trusts, which helped structure the easements and raise funds; and federal programs that provided matching funds for habitat restoration and floodplain protection.Under the agreement, most of the land will no longer be farmed. Instead, it will be restored to floodplain forest, wetlands and grasslands, with drainage ditches and levees removed or breached to allow the rivers to reconnect with their historic floodplain.What the restoration will look likeOver the coming years, crews will begin the work of transforming the former farmland: Planting native trees such as silver maple, cottonwood, willow and oak to re-establish floodplain forest; restoring wetland areas by reshaping low spots and allowing them to fill with water naturally; removing or modifying levees and ditches so the river can spread out during high flows instead of being confined to a narrow channel; and establishing native grasses and forbs in higher areas to provide habitat for pollinators, grassland birds and other wildlife.The goal is not to create a pristine wilderness, but a working floodplain that benefits both people and nature. The land will be open for public hunting, fishing, birdwatching and hiking, while also serving as a natural buffer that reduces flood peaks for downstream communities.Why this matters for Wisconsin’s riversThe Hoesly floodplain is just one piece of a larger puzzle along the Wisconsin and Kickapoo rivers. Decades of levees, channelisation and drainage have disconnected many rivers from their natural floodplains, speeding up water flow and increasing flood risks downstream. By restoring nearly 2,000 acres of bottomland, the project provides more space for floodwaters to spread out, reducing pressure on levees and towns downstream. It also improves water quality by allowing sediments and nutrients to settle out in the floodplain instead of flowing directly into the river. And, creates critical habitat for species that depend on large, connected floodplain forests and wetlands.For state agencies and conservation groups, the deal is a model for how private landowners, government and nonprofits can work together to address both flooding and habitat loss.A family’s legacy redefinedFor the Hoesly family, the conservation agreement is both an ending and a beginning. It marks the end of an era in which the bottomland was primarily a corn and soybean farm, managed against the river. But it also establishes a new legacy: one in which the family is credited with protecting one of the largest remaining floodplain complexes in the region.Family members have said that the decision was not easy, but that it felt right given the realities of climate change, flooding and the changing economics of farming. They see the protected land as a gift to future generations—both their own descendants and the broader public who will be able to enjoy the restored landscape.A sign of things to come?As climate change drives more extreme weather across the Midwest, similar stories are likely to play out in other flood-prone farming regions. The Hoesly deal shows that permanent conservation can be a viable alternative to endless investment in flood control on land that is increasingly unsuited to intensive agriculture.For now, the fields along the Wisconsin and Kickapoo rivers are being replanted not with corn, but with trees, grasses and the promise of a river allowed to behave like a river again. And a farming family that once fought to keep the water off their land is now helping to welcome it back.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: SC: BCI chair's tenure is for 2 years, can't be made 5 years by own resolution
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: With two PILs heaping allegations against functioning of advocates regulatory body Bar Council of India and questioning legality of its Apr.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: With two PILs heaping allegations against functioning of advocates regulatory body Bar Council of India and questioning legality of its Apr 2025 resolution giving a five-year term to chairperson Manan Kumar Mishra, Supreme Court Wednesday said no resolution can override the statutorily prescribed two-year term.A bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said even if a BCI resolution generously gives a five-year term to the chairperson, his tenure ex-facie cannot exceed beyond 2027 notwithstanding the legality of the resolution.Petitioners question lavish spendNo resolution can alter the statutorily provided two-year tenure for the chairperson,” the bench said.The petitioners questioned the lavish spending of crores on felicitation functions, organising seminars and alleged misuse of Bar Council of India trust funds to open law colleges in states and demanded a high-level inquiry into the council’s affairs.The bench said the elections to state bar councils had been completed and directed the completion of co-option of women members by the high court chief justices concerned in consultation with newly elected members within two weeks.The entire composition of state bar councils, including co-opted women members, would be notified within a week thereafter.It said the newly formed state bar councils would elect their representative to BCI a week later to enable the latter to conduct fresh election of the chairperson and the vice-chairperson.Till then, the BCI governing body would act in a pro tem manner and not take any policy decision.On the bench’s suggestion, the council volunteered to invite the attorney general and the solicitor general to its meetings.Mishra has been chairperson of BCI since Nov 9, 2014.The petitioners asked whether a statutory authority entrusted with “regulating more than 20 lakh advocates, administering legal education, conducting the All India Bar Examination, exercising disciplinary jurisdiction, and safeguarding independence of the legal profession, can lawfully permit prolonged concentration of regulatory authority in the same hands articles.title: Hands-Free Phone Laws by State: Is It Illegal to Hold Your Phone While Driving?
articles.summary: More than 30 states now have hands-free phone laws banning handheld cell phone use while driving. See if your state made the list, what the penalties are and the best products to help you stay compliant.
articles.body: If you’ve caught yourself reaching for your phone at a red light lately, you might want to think twice — depending on where you live, that quick grab could cost you. More than 30 states now have some version of a “hands-free” or “no-touch” phone law on the books, making it illegal to hold or manually use a cell phone while driving. The laws vary from state to state — some ban any handheld use altogether, while others allow limited actions like a single tap to answer a call. Regardless, the goal is the same: to keep drivers’ eyes on the road and hands on the wheel. For many, this shift means rethinking driving habits, including the urge to check directions and answer calls while on the go. Keep reading to find out whether your state has a no-touch phone law, what the penalties look like if you’re caught breaking it and to discover a few products that can help you stay hands-free — and compliant — behind the wheel. Want more from NBC Selected? Sign up for our newsletter, The Selection, and shop smarter. What is the no-touch phone law? “No-touch laws are the evolution of texting-while-driving laws,” says Ryan McMahon, senior vice president of strategy and corporate development at Cambridge Mobile Telematics, the world’s largest telematics and AI service provider focused on driver safety. “Those laws were written when texting was the primary concern. Today, drivers are scrolling, using social media, changing music, reading emails and doing countless other things on their phones.” The no-touch phone law (also called a hands-free driving law) makes it illegal for drivers to hold or manually operate a cell phone while behind the wheel. It varies by state, but generally hands-free functions like voice commands and Bluetooth are permitted. “These laws also make enforcement simpler,” says McMahon. “An officer doesn’t have to determine whether someone holding a phone was texting, scrolling or doing something else.” Most of these laws do carve out exceptions for emergency calls to 911, use by law enforcement and first responders, and phone use while a vehicle is safely stopped or parked. Which states have the no-touch phone law? As of 2026, no-touch phone laws are the majority rule in the U.S. rather than the exception. The Governors Highway Safety Association reports that 33 states (at the time of publishing we counted more) plus Washington D.C. now ban handheld phone use for all drivers, generally prohibiting drivers from holding a device at all while behind the wheel. The exact details of these laws vary by state — some allow a single tap to answer a call, while others, like California, have clarified that drivers may not touch a phone at all while driving, even when stopped at a red light. Each state approaches this legislation differently, so it’s tough to put together a comprehensive list, but the below states are commonly recognized as the ones with the more formalized and stringent laws. AlabamaAlaskaArizonaCaliforniaColoradoConnecticutDelawareGeorgiaHawaiiIdahoIllinoisIndianaIowaLouisianaMaineMarylandMassachusettsMichiganMinnesotaMissouriNebraskaNevadaNew HampshireNew JerseyNew YorkNorth CarolinaOhioOregonPennsylvaniaRhode IslandSouth CarolinaTennesseeUtahVermontVirginiaWashingtonWest VirginiaDistrict of Columbia What happens if you break the no-touch phone law? Penalties for violating a no-touch phone law vary by state, but in reviewing the laws in various states I found that most follow a similar pattern: a fine for a first offense, followed by steeper fines, license points (penalties added to your driving record), or both for repeat violations. Fines commonly start in the range of $50–$150 for a first offense and can climb well past $200–$500 for second or subsequent violations within a set period, sometimes with added court fees. A handful of states (including Alaska and Georgia) escalate to misdemeanor charges or license suspension for habitual offenders. Beyond the ticket itself, a citation can have longer-term financial consequences. Points on your license or a moving violation on your record often lead to higher auto insurance premiums, sometimes for several years, according to experts. Because penalty amounts, point systems, and enforcement rules differ by state — and change fairly often as legislatures update distracted driving laws — it’s worth confirming the exact penalties for your state through its DMV website. The best phone mounts for your car Using Bluetooth and a phone mount so your phone is easily accessible for a quick swipe (if your state allows it), is a good way to abide by no-touch phone laws, according to McMahon. “Just remember the goal is to minimize interaction with the phone while driving,” he adds. Below, I rounded up devices that either help you mount your phone so it is within reach but out of your hands or that help utilize your car’s Bluetooth system. I focused on items that have at least a four-star average rating from thousands of customers. This little dongle plugs into your car’s USB port and converts factory wired CarPlay into wireless CarPlay — giving you hands-free access to navigation, music, and calls via voice commands, so your phone can stay in your pocket the entire drive. This phone mount attaches securely to your dashboard, windshield, or air vent using a powerful reusable suction cup system. It features a 360-degree swivel head, extendable telescopic arm, and adjustable clamp that fits phones between 4 and 7 inches (which covers most iPhones and Androids). Compatible with iPhones that have MagSafe capability, this dashboard mount snaps your phone into place and rotates 360 degrees, letting you navigate or take calls hands-free or with minimal touching of your phone. With a bendable 14-inch gooseneck arm and heavy-duty suction cup, this mount attaches to your windshield or dashboard and holds your phone exactly where you need it to navigate or take calls without ever picking it up. The adjustable clip fits both iPhone and Androids. This mount attaches securely to your dashboard and rotates a full 360 degrees, letting you angle your phone for easy viewing whether you place it vertically or horizontally. It is compatible with most phones and it comes with reusable adhesive in case you need to move it. What does the no-touch phone law allow you to do with your phone in the car? Even though no-touch laws restrict handling your phone, they don’t require you to ignore it altogether — they just push all interaction into hands-free territory. South Carolina’s law, for example, allows an earpiece or a voice-based device worn on the wrist, and drivers can talk hands-free as long as they aren’t holding or supporting the phone with any part of their body. In practice, this means most states allow you to make and receive calls through Bluetooth, a car’s built-in system, or a speakerphone, as long as you’re not gripping the device. Voice commands — like asking Siri or Google Assistant to place a call, send a text, or pull up directions — are generally fine too, since the point is keeping your hands and eyes off the device, not banning phone functions outright. Mounted phones are typically allowed as well (and encouraged by a number of states), so you can still use your phone as a GPS if it’s secured to your dashboard or windshield, provided you’re not picking it up or manually typing while driving. Some states, like New Jersey, also permit a single tap or swipe to start or end a call or activate navigation before you start driving, while others require the entire interaction to be voice-activated. Most laws also carve out exceptions for emergencies, such as calling 911 to report a crash or dangerous situation. Again, because the laws vary by state, it’s best to check the DMV site to read the parameters for your state. articles.title: DAVID MARCUS: Canada sees Trump trade war as ‘life and death’ while Americans barely notice
articles.summary: Expert Gary Mar warns Canada faces bigger sticks in a tariff battle with the United States as the Sept. 7 trade deal deadline approaches fast.
articles.body: Gary Mar is a guy who knows a thing or two about trade between the United States and Canada. As the president of the Canada West Foundation and a former minister dealing with trade for the Province of Alberta, he’s seen a lot — but nothing quite like the current asymmetrical trade dispute between the two nations. America and our neighbors to the north face a Sept. 7 deadline to reach a new trade deal, or see crippling sanctions go into effect on both sides. But the citizens of each country are not treating this looming crisis the same way at all. "The 49th parallel [is] like a two-way mirror," Mar told Fox News Digital this week. "Canadians look through it, and they see Americans. But Americans look at the same mirror, and they see themselves. So we get much more information on what’s going on in the United States than Americans ever get... with respect to Canada." CANADIAN PM TELLS TRUMP TO 'STOP TRYING TO BE TOUGH' IN TRADE FIGHT This is a fair assessment. For example, most Americans likely do not know that, since President Donald Trump took office, Canadian grocery stores and pharmacies have aggressive signs pointing out what products were made in America, to boycott them. Nothing remotely like that has happened stateside. Likewise, in the Great White North, these trade flare-ups are by far the biggest story in the country, fueled by a state-run media that might even hate Trump more than our domestic liberal media does. In America, this story is lucky to hit the C-slot of a cable news show. ‘CAPTAIN CANADA’ FIREBRAND UNLOADS ON TRUMP WITH PROFANE ONE-LINER AS TRADE WAR ESCALATES The point is that, from the perspective of public opinion intensity, there is just no comparison. Canadians think they are in an existential fight, while most Americans barely know it is happening. This asymmetry also applies to the political realities facing Trump and Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney. Trump faces some Democrats all but siding with Canada. Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, for instance, said this week, "If you start a trade war with Canada, you are the a------." FOX NEWS POLL: A SENATE BATTLE LOOMS IN MICHIGAN I asked Mar if this kind of thing could happen in Canada — could conservative politicians like Pierre Poilievre come out in favor of Trump — and not surprisingly, the answer is no. Speaking on the Canadian right, Mar said, "They can be critical of how the liberal government is conducting their relationship with the U.S., but it would be very difficult for the conservatives to say, ‘We agree with Donald Trump.’" TRUMP TRADE CHIEF WARNS CANADA WALKED AWAY FROM 'THE BEST DEAL' TO TRIGGER 50% U.S. TARIFFS It is reasonable to assume that this rally-round-the-maple-leaf moment of unity in Canada accrues to Carney’s benefit in negotiations, and Mar acknowledges that. As former House Speaker Newt Gingrich has suggested, Carney may be trying to game the U.S. midterms by punishing swing states like Maine and Michigan economically via tariffs. But not everything is slanted against Trump in these negotiations. The biggest asymmetry of all is the sheer power of the U.S. economy, and Mar had some sobering words for Canada regarding an all-out tariff battle. TRUMP'S CANADA TARIFF FIGHT REACHES CRITICAL POINT AS HOUSE GOP SUMMONS TRADE CHIEF "What I see now is a discussion of who can inflict more pain on the other side," Mar said. "The difficulty for Canada getting involved in a tit-for-tat, or a stick-swinging incident — as we might use the metaphor from hockey — is that [the] U.S. has more sticks to swing. They’ve got bigger sticks to swing, and their sticks have spikes on them." That about sums it up. A POPULAR COCKTAIL HAS A TRUMP TRADE PROBLEM YOU PROBABLY DIDN’T KNOW ABOUT Both Canada and the United States have good reasons to just make a deal by the upcoming deadline and put this all behind them, at least for now. But with each side blaming the other for the breakdown in talks, it may be too heavy a lift. If talks fail, the real question won’t be how it impacts the midterms, but rather, whether it leads Canada to lean more heavily on other partners such as China, and whether Venezuela can actually be stable enough to attract oil companies away from friendly, old Canada.
