articles.title: Government bodies differ, Centre to test green crackers afresh
articles.summary: India News: NEW DELHI: As two govt organisations took contradictory stands on commercial production of next-generation green firecrackers - with Council of Scient.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: As two govt organisations took contradictory stands on commercial production of next-generation green firecrackers - with Council of Scientific and Industrial Research-NEERI approving new formulations and Central Pollution Control Board objecting - Centre Wednesday told Supreme Court that it intended to conduct fresh tests to assess the harmful impact of the use of barium.Additional solicitor general Aishwarya Bhati told a bench of Justices M M Sundresh and Augustine George Masih that govt, after consulting stakeholders, had decided to conduct the tests in New Delhi, Bhopal, Kolkata and Chennai.Centre had asked CSIR-NEERI to develop green/low-emission fireworks - with particulate matter (PM) emission reduction of more than 50% - in association with manufacturers. Tamil Nadu Fireworks and Amorces Manufacturers' Association (Tanfama) devised new-generation formulation crackers with a reduced quantity of barium salts/nitrates in combination with other oxidisers.In a report, CSIR-NEERI said with the new formulations, emission reductions achieved for PM10 and PM2.5 were between 45% and 60%, and recommended that the formulations for light-emission fireworks (such as flowerpots, sparklers, chakkars, pencils, twinkling stars and their hybrids) be considered for commercial production.It also approved the manufacture of 'joined crackers', known as 'ladis', which have been banned by a court order. The report said there was a reduction in PM emissions by approximately 30% and a reduction in solid waste generation by up to 32% for joined crackers.CPCB asked how barium nitrate could be used in crackers when it was banned by SC. "This court, vide order dated Oct 23, 2018, has expressly banned the use of barium salts in firecrackers and, therefore, any formulation involving barium compounds, even in reduced quantities, is in contravention of the said order," it said in its communication to govt."The reported reduction in PM10 and PM2.5 levels has not been comparatively assessed with (i) improved low-emission crackers and (ii) green crackers formulated entirely without barium, rendering the claim incomplete and inconclusive," it added.The petitioners, on whose plea polluting firecrackers were banned, submitted that the court had over the years passed eight orders to ban the use of barium and its use in cracker manufacturing could not be allowed.SC asked Centre to get suggestions from experts, saying the court had no expertise in these matters.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Far-left writer ripped in viral debate over 'absurd' claim that capitalism is tied to White supremacy
articles.summary: Jemele Hill doubled down on her claim linking capitalism to white supremacy after a CNN panel clash with Kmele Foster over the issue.
articles.body: Liberal Atlantic writer Jemele Hill doubled down after suggesting that capitalism was linked to White supremacy, during a heated clash with another panelist on CNN on Tuesday. "It's one thing to not think capitalism isn't working ideally. It's another thing entirely to insist that it is oppressive, that it is bound up with White supremacy," Kmele Foster, a podcast host, said. "How is it not?" Hill pressed. The panelists were responding to newly unearthed 2020 comments, first reported by CNN, in which Texas Senate candidate James Talarico described capitalism as an "oppressive system" that is linked to White supremacy and climate change and needs to be dismantled. MODERN CAPITALISM IS TURNING 250, TOO. WE NEED TO REMIND AMERICANS WHY IT’S IMPORTANT "I've always preferred Adam Smith's description of capitalism as the natural system of liberty, the idea that people can own property, that they can exchange it freely with one another for profit, that they can find ways to put their resources to good use, those private property," Foster continued. He added, "And profit in a way that is actually beneficial to everyone else, that there can be gains from trade that are mutually beneficial. These are foundational ideas that have created more wealth than any other system in human history. That is what capitalism is, that's not White supremacy." "Do you think capitalism has always worked that way?" Hill asked Foster. "I've actually just described the basic facts of economics," Foster responded. "Slavery is an institution that is older than writing. It predates capitalism. The notion that White supremacy and all these other things are bound up with capitalism in an intrinsic and fundamental way is so absurd and laughable, it barely needs to be defended." Foster asked Hill to substantiate her argument and asked multiple times about the "the White supremacist dynamic of private property." "But you're talking about capitalism in the purest form of how it was intended to work versus how it's actually working. It's not working," Hill argued. Hill was called out on social media by other media commentators and hosts. Political commentor Mary Katharine Ham said, "Kmele: ‘You actually have to articulate what the connection is.' Hill writes for the Atlantic and has years of TV experience, but it didn’t occur to her she would ever need to, and she isn’t prepared to." Podcast host Stephen Miller noted that Hill worked for the Atlantic and wrote, "She is a staff writer for one of the most prestigious neoliberal publications in the country and she's never been once challenged on any of her ideas like this." JEMELE HILL FALSELY CLAIMS ELECTORAL COLLEGE IS ENTIRELY 'ROOTED IN SLAVERY' AND IT COST KAMALA THE ELECTION Liberal commentator Leigh McGowan also made the case that capitalism was not working during the exchange. "I think that's the problem. I think the problem is it's not working well, today. I think for a long time that is a great way to describe it. Adam Smith capitalism, if we had that, that would be totally different," she said. "We have got to a place where we have deregulated everything so much that only a certain handful of people are actually succeeding in this version of capitalism." Socialism has gained popularity among younger voters, according to a Fox News Poll from March. The survey found a record 38% believed it would be a good thing for the United States to move away from capitalism and in the direction of socialism — up from 32% in 2022, the last time the question was asked. In 2010, a low of 18% backed socialism. Hill appeared to double down after the exchange. "America was built on the institution of slavery. It is how America became a world economic power — the buying and selling of people being tied to the economy. That is effectively white supremacy, since it was a race-based system. Fast-forward to other economic policies that were guided by race — housing, employment, etc. There were rules that prevented Black people from equally participating in the free economy. In fact, one of the most glaring features of American capitalism is racial inequality. The racial wealth gap exists because specific policies were put in place to suppress economic participation. So yes, capitalism is tied to White supremacy," Hill said in a post to X that followed the CNN panel debate. Hill did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for further comment. Talarico made his 2020 comments at the Austin Sierra Club during a virtual candidate forum while serving his first term as a state representative. His answer came in response to a question about what lawmakers could do to address climate change in communities of color, according to CNN's K-File. "I am so thankful that you asked this question and also thankful that young activists have really drawn the link between climate change and White supremacy and capitalism in our country," Talarico said. "And I think only ending the ways that all three of those oppressive systems work together are we gonna be able to begin the process of dismantling them." During the same event, Talarico said the oil and gas industry was not going to last. CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE "We all know that Texas has been a leader in oil and gas, but in many ways that’s like being the leader in cassette tapes in the 1980s," Talarico later said, responding to another question. "That industry is not gonna last. And if we wanna ensure we have an economy that’s gonna work for our children and our children’s children, we gotta be ahead of the curve and Texas has to lead instead of follow on this issue." "James supports the oil and gas industry and believes in an all of the above energy strategy that protects Texas oil and gas jobs. He’s already said he missed the mark on some of his past statements, but Ken Paxton is clipping a few old, cringey comments to distract from his career of corruption that includes being impeached by his own party, enriching himself and his billionaire mega-donors, and using his office to protect pedophiles and animal abusers," Talarico campaign spokesperson JT Ennis told Fox News Digital in a statement regarding the oil and gas industry remarks. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Ennis' statement also said Talarico is a "proud capitalist," and "agrees with the majority of Texans that racism, natural disasters, and a billionaire-controlled economy are all problems we need to address." "James has already said he missed the mark on some of his past statements, while Ken Paxton has refused to address his comments that the school shooting in Uvalde was ‘God’s plan’ and that Texas’ abortion ban is good for interstate commerce," the statement continued. The Democratic state representative is facing off against Republican Ken Paxton in the midterm elections for U.S. Senate in November.

articles.title: Two Palestinians killed as settlers, Israeli forces raid West Bank village
articles.summary: Teenagers killed in settlers attack on al-Mughayyer as West Bank violence continues.
articles.body:
Two Palestinian teenagers have been killed during a raid by settlers and Israeli forces in the occupied West Bank.

The killings occurred during a raid in al-Mughayyir on Wednesday. The village has been the site of repeated attacks by illegal Israeli settlers and Israeli forces in recent months.

The Palestinian Wafa news agency, citing the head of the village council, identified those killed as Mohammad Na’ssan and Khalil Abu Aliya, both 19 years old.

As residents tried to confront the settlers, Israeli soldiers opened fire on the residents, critically wounding two young men, he said. They later died from the wounds.

Sources from the village told Al Jazeera that snipers had taken positions on rooftops in the village ahead of the killings.

Since the beginning of 2026, at least 79 Palestinians, including 19 children, have been killed in the occupied West Bank by settlers or Israeli forces, according to the United Nations Office for the coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA).

At least 1,870 Palestinian have been wounded.

Settler attacks in al-Mughayyer have largely focused on the village’s only access road, where vehicles have regularly been targeted, according to OCHA.

In a recent incident on August 20, eleven Palestinians were wounded in an attack.

On Tuesday, Israeli forces fired tear gas into a mosque in Madama, leaving those gathered coughing for air, according to footage verified by Al Jazeera.

Hours earlier, Israeli settlers tried to set fire to another mosque in the nearby town of Bazariya.

The surging settler violence, often supported by Israeli forces, has roiled Israel’s allies.

Last month, a three-week settler siege of a Palestinian home in Qusra, south of Nablus, prompted a rare rebuke from United States ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, a staunch supporter of Israel and its West Bank settlements.

The European Union, meanwhile, has been weighing a ban on settler-made goods.

In late August, the United Nations Special Coordinator for the Middle East Process ad interim, Dr Ramiz Alakbarov, said that settler attacks have continued with “virtually no accountability”.

Experts, including United Nations Special Rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories Francesca Albanese, have increasingly said the attacks fit the definition of progroms.

articles.title: The Gentlemen: Stars of Netflix show react to Meghan speculation at series 2 premiere
articles.summary: The world premiere for series 2 of the Netflix drama took place on Wednesday night in London.
articles.body:
It has been almost two weeks since reports emerged that the Duchess of Sussex was in talks for a role in The Gentlemen.

At the world premiere for series two of the Netflix show on Wednesday night, stars including Maya Jama, Hugh Bonneville and Theo James remained tight-lipped about the prospect of Meghan joining the cast.

“It’s fascinating to watch, but ultimately it’s a lot of rumour,” James told BBC News, while Jama said: “I’d be the last person to know!”

The show’s executive producer said he didn't want to say yes or no to the reports about Meghan, but added they were looking forward to “more energy and surprises” to come.

The Gentlemen, a comedy action series about a duke turned drug baron, created by Guy Ritchie, was a major hit when it first dropped in 2024.

The show has officially been greenlit for a third series. Talks with Meghan are understood to be in the early stages , but the details of the discussions and any role she might be offered have not yet been revealed.

The drizzle cleared up as stars arrived at the Guildhall, with Vinnie Jones, Kaya Scodelario, Joely Richardson and Ray Winstone all in attendance.

When asked about the reports regarding Meghan, Jones said he's heard “only what you have".

But he joked: “We’ve got a lot of pretty women in this. So I’m not sure there’s room for any more.”

"Way above my pay grade," Scodelario said, while Bonneville commented he had “no idea” if there was any truth to the rumours.

Jama, meanwhile, said as a newcomer herself to the cast, she had no tips to share with Meghan.

“Oh my God, she’s a seasoned actor. I have no advice for her. She knows what she’s doing,” added Jama.

Ritchie, who also attended the premiere, did not speak to the press. But writer and executive producer Matthew Read told BBC News they were looking forward to "bringing up more energy and surprises in series two and further on in the series”.

"I just don't think it's right to speculate at this stage, so I wouldn't like to say yes or no,” he added.

In the first series, Eddie Halstead (played by James) inherited his wealthy family's country estate following his father's death, much to the fury of his older brother Freddy. He then discovers the estate is partly being used to grow cannabis for an extremely successful underground drug empire.

This time around, the criminal enterprise is expanding out of the British countryside and into the lush lakeside setting of Italy.

On the second series, James said: "If you're going to do it, you've got to make sure it's better.

"So we worked, I hope, pretty hard to make sure we evolve the world. It was more complex, and we had more character development."

That was echoed by Scodelario, who plays one of the show's toughest and most assured characters, Susie Glass. She runs the cannabis farm under the estate's grounds.

"We've really tried to raise the stakes as much as possible," she said. "Some of the episodes take a much darker turn, but we still have the fun and the joy that everyone really liked about it."

Bonneville, another newcomer to the cast for series two, said working with Ritchie was "wonderfully chaotic, but with a great purpose in mind".

The actor, who previously starred in Downton Abbey, also joked there was no difference between the period drama and the criminal underworld of The Gentlemen. "It was exactly the same world," he said.

"No, it was fun to enter this slightly skewed world of the perverted aristocracy up to no good," he added.

"I'm sure it was going on at Downton Abbey, but now the lid is lifted on what really happens in these stately homes."

The Gentlemen series two is released on Netflix on 3 September.
